Going by the standard literature: embedding real-world information networks is harder than embedding small ones because they are very large (millions of nodes and edges), so methods that build or factorize full adjacency or similarity matrices become computationally and memory-intensive. These networks are also sparse, heterogeneous, and noisy, and they evolve over time, which makes global, exact optimization impractical. DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014) addresses this by sampling many short truncated random walks from each node and treating each walk as a 'sentence' over node 'words', then training a Skip-gram model (word2vec-style) to predict a node's neighbours within a window. This is scalable and captures local neighbourhood structure and higher-order co-occurrence. One correction to the question's premise: DeepWalk uses uniform random walks, not non-random ones. Its signal beyond direct adjacency comes from the co-occurrence statistics of nodes that appear close together on walks, which reflect multi-hop and community structure rather than only immediate topology. If Passage B describes biased walks (such as node2vec's p and q parameters), that would be a different, non-uniform extension of this idea.
